sections.overview: The mahi-mahi, or common dolphinfish, is a fast-growing, open-ocean fish found in tropical and warm temperate seas worldwide. Despite its English name, it is a fish, not a dolphin.
sections.identification: Its laterally flattened, streamlined body carries a single dorsal fin that runs from above the head almost to the deeply forked tail. The back is metallic blue-green, the sides flash gold and silver with dark spots, and these vivid colours fade quickly after death. Adult males develop a high, squared forehead, while females have a more rounded head. The related pompano dolphinfish, Coryphaena equiselis, is deeper-bodied and has a trapezoid-shaped tooth patch on the tongue; C. hippurus has an oval patch. NOAA reports that the species can reach almost 2.1 m and 40 kg. These are upper limits, not typical adult measurements; the source does not give a sex-specific weight range or body width.
sections.habitat: It lives near the surface of offshore tropical, subtropical and warm temperate waters across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans, entering the Mediterranean occasionally. Floating seaweed rafts and other drifting objects offer shelter and concentrated feeding grounds, especially for smaller fish. Adults commonly reach about one metre; rare specimens approach 2.1 metres.
sections.diet: A daytime predator, the mahi-mahi pursues small pelagic fish such as flying fish and juvenile tuna, as well as squid, crabs and other drifting invertebrates. Its fast swimming and broad prey menu let it exploit abundant food around floating weed and in open water.
sections.behavior: Young fish commonly school, whereas older individuals are often solitary; large males tend to range in open water, while females and smaller males often gather near floating objects. Its changing colour pattern is striking in life but fades rapidly when the fish is landed.
sections.reproduction: Both sexes can mature within their first year, at about four to five months in Atlantic populations. Females release eggs into the water repeatedly during the warm spawning season; in the Atlantic, spawning occurs beneath floating Sargassum mats.
sections.ecology: Mahi-mahi transfer energy from small fish and drifting invertebrates to larger predators, including tuna, marlin, sailfish, swordfish and marine mammals. Floating algae serve as juvenile shelter and feeding habitat, linking this open-water predator to drifting surface communities.
sections.conservation: Its global conservation status is Least Concern. Fishing pressure and longline bycatch of turtles or marine mammals are concerns; Atlantic stock assessments remain incomplete in several U.S. regions.
